title: Four thoughts that turn the mind
hookLine: precious human life, death, karma, the faults of samsara

cards: A doctor's call. A birthday with a zero on the end. A friend who was fine last month, and isn't.

Most people change direction only after a jolt like that. For a week or two, everything looks different: what matters, what doesn't, how you want to spend your hours. Then the feeling fades and the old grooves take over.
Tibetan teachers noticed this long ago, and built the jolt into the very start of the path, on purpose, so it wouldn't depend on bad news.

teach.b: In Tibetan practice, four reflections come before everything else, and people return to them for a lifetime. First, precious human life.

Tibetan teachers borrow an image the Buddha gives in the Pali discourses: a blind turtle in the great ocean rises to the surface once every hundred years, and a wooden yoke with one hole drifts on the waves.
The turtle will put its head through that hole, the Buddha says, sooner than a being who has fallen into the lower realms will win back a human birth.
So this life, with the time and freedom to learn anything at all, is rare. Second, death and impermanence.

teach.h: DEATH IS CERTAIN, ITS TIME IS NOT.
teach.b: Death is certain; its time is not.
Third, karma: actions have results, and the small ones add up.
Fourth, the faults of samsara, the round of birth and death: even the good parts don't last, and chasing them never quite satisfies.

The twelfth-century teacher Gampopa taught all four in a well-known book, and the preliminary practices set them in this order, which matters. First you see how lucky you are. Then how short the time is.
Then how much your actions count. Then that more chasing won't fix it. Together, they swing the mind around, like a boat in the current, toward the path.
Now look back at the week. For a while. The question is still open.
Virtue, calm, wisdom. The elders' day. Then the climb: the diamond vehicle.
The jewel in the lotus. The wind carries it.

how: Tibetan Buddhists often recite and reflect on the four thoughts at the start of each practice session, and they form the first part of the preliminary practices (ngöndro) taught in all the Tibetan schools.

o: the teacher who taught the four thoughts
the first king to bring Buddhism to Tibet
the Tibetan word for the round of rebirth

p: certain, but its time is not

s: the blind turtle image comes from the Pali discourses
the Buddha uses it to show how rare a human birth is.
the four thoughts are for advanced students only
they come first, at the start of the path, and people return to them for life.
the order of the four doesn't matter
luck first, then urgency, then care, then seeing that chasing won't fix it.

games.q: you've just heard that human life is precious and death's timing unknown. a Tibetan teacher asks what you'll do with that. which answer fits the four thoughts?
o: panic and try to do everything at once.
let it turn the mind toward what matters, steadily.
games.why: the four thoughts aren't meant to frighten but to turn the mind, like a boat in the current, toward the path.

practice: Choose one of the four and stay with it: for precious human life, picture the turtle and the yoke, then look at your own hands, here, with time to sit; for death, rest in the thought that this breath is one of a limited number.
Don't push toward a feeling; let the thought sit beside you the way you'd sit beside a friend. When the mind wanders, return to the one you chose.

wordCard.voice: Gampopa. The twelfth-century teacher who taught the four thoughts in a well-known book: precious human life, death, karma, and the faults of samsara.

orig.note: Tibetan blo ldog rnam bzhi: blo (mind) + ldog (turn back) + rnam bzhi (the four): the four thoughts that turn the mind.

carryVoice: Your line: turn the mind. Four thoughts, and the boat swings toward the path. That's the week.
